pr.title: Only compute recursive callees once.
pr.description:
Inlining MIR in a cyclic call graph may create query cycles, which are ICEs. The current implementation `mir_callgraph_reachable(inlining_candidate, being_optimized)` checks if calling `inlining_candidate` may cycle back to `being_optimized` that we are currently inlining into.

This PR replaces this device with query `mir_callgraph_cyclic(being_optimized)` which searches the call graph for all cycles going back to `being_optimized`, and returns the set of functions involved in those cycles.

This is a tradeoff:
- in the current implementation, we perform more walks, but shallower;
- in this new implementation, we perform fewer walks, but exhaust the graph.

I'd have liked to compute this using some kind of SCC, but generic parameters make resolution path-dependent, so usual graph algorithms do not apply.

processing.reason: The PR is a cost/performance refactor of the MIR inliner's cycle-avoidance query, not a semantic miscompile. The frozen analysis itself states: "This is not a semantic miscompile; the historical transformation was the old per-candidate reachability query. Its deficiency is cost/recomputation." The patch has two equivalent decision procedures: old `mir_callgraph_reachable((callee, caller))` walks from a candidate and returns true upon reaching the caller (or on recursion-limit overflow), while new `mir_callgraph_cyclic(caller).contains(&callee)` computes the cyclic-callee set once per caller and membership-tests the same candidate. Both are intended to yield the same inlining decision ("caller might be reachable from callee"). The provided historical material contains only compiler-side query/caching changes (`inline.rs`, `inline/cycle.rs`, `query/mod.rs`, `lib.rs`) and no source-level value transformation or corrected program output to encode. Encoding an arbitrary inlining-decision difference—e.g., around the pessimistic recursion-limit branch or path-dependent generic resolution—would be inventing a wrong transformation not justified as a semantic bug by the PR. Since no source-grounded semantic counterexample exists, no valid original/transformed pair can be produced.

analysis.summary: The MIR inliner's cycle-avoidance check was changed from a per-candidate `mir_callgraph_reachable((callee, caller))` boolean query to a cached `mir_callgraph_cyclic(caller)` query returning every local function involved in a cycle back to the caller. The new query walks the call graph once per caller and memoizes the cyclic-callee set (arena/disk cached), instead of repeating a graph walk for every inlining candidate. Both `Inline` and `ForceInline` participate because recursion is only followed for instances whose pass is enabled.
analysis.originalLogic: Before the change, `mir_callgraph_reachable(key: (ty::Instance<'tcx>, LocalDefId)) -> bool` checked one candidate at a time: "Check whether the function has any recursion that could cause the inliner to trigger a cycle." Given an inlining candidate instance and the caller being optimized, it walked from the candidate and returned true if it reached the caller, or stopped early on a path. The inliner called it as `inliner.tcx().mir_callgraph_reachable((callee, caller_def_id.expect_local()))` and refused inlining when it returned true. The PR notes this performs "more walks, but shallower" because the same reachability question is recomputed for each candidate.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: This is not a semantic miscompile; the historical transformation was the old per-candidate reachability query. Its deficiency is cost/recomputation: for every local inlining candidate it re-walked the call graph to answer the same caller-specific question. The PR replaces that with a single query `mir_callgraph_cyclic(caller)` that returns the whole set of local callees in cycles back to the caller, then tests membership with `.contains(&callee_def_id)`. The new logic also factors out `should_recurse` to decide which instances are worth following, records every callee on a found recursion path into `involved`, and pessimistically treats hitting the recursion limit as recursion. A separate agent should model the transformation as old "walk per candidate and stop at caller" versus new "walk once per caller, collect all cyclic local callees, then membership-test each candidate"; it should not invent a wrong inlining decision just to produce different output.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust crates whose local functions have MIR available and whose call graph may contain cycles back to the function currently being optimized. The domain includes mutually recursive functions, generic instantiations (resolution is path-dependent), shims, constructors, intrinsics/virtual calls, and drop glue. Resolution uses `typing_env = ty::TypingEnv::post_analysis(tcx, root)` and `ty::Instance::try_resolve`; unresolved or non-normalizable callees are skipped. Non-local callees are excluded from the returned involved set because "Calling `optimized_mir` of a non-local definition cannot cycle."
analysis.trigger: While `Inline` is deciding whether to inline a local callee into the caller currently being optimized, the callee may transitively call back to that caller. Inlining it would make building/optimizing MIR re-enter the same query, so `check_mir_is_available` must reject it with "caller might be reachable from callee". The new query is triggered once per caller as `mir_callgraph_cyclic(caller_def_id.expect_local())`.
preconditions: The caller is a local definition and the inliner is not in a `FnOnce` lang-item context: `if let Some(callee_def_id) = callee_def_id.as_local() && !inliner.tcx().is_lang_item(inliner.tcx().parent(caller_def_id), rustc_hir::LangItem::FnOnce)`.

MIR inlining or force-inlining is enabled for the candidate, as decided by `crate::pm::should_run_pass(tcx, &crate::inline::Inline, crate::pm::Optimizations::Allowed) || ForceInline::should_run_pass_for_callee(tcx, callee.def.def_id())`.
The root passed to `mir_callgraph_cyclic` must not be a constructor: `assert!(!tcx.is_constructor(root.to_def_id()), ...)`.

The candidate instance must be one that can actually carry callable MIR: `Item` with MIR available, or supported shims; intrinsics, virtual calls, `FnPtrAddrShim`, MIR-less items, and parameterized drop glue are skipped.
A call-graph recursion limiter is used: `let recursion_limit = tcx.recursion_limit() / 2;`, and exceeding it is treated pessimistically as a possible cycle.
pitfalls: Do not use ordinary SCC/graph algorithms here: the PR states that generic parameters make resolution path-dependent, so a naive cross-path SCC may be unsound or inapplicable.
Do not drop the per-instance `seen` set or recursion limiter while exhausting the graph; without them the walk can recurse forever or blow the stack. The code also uses `ensure_sufficient_stack`.
Do not include non-local callees in the involved set; only local definitions can cause an `optimized_mir` query cycle. The code inserts via `callee.def_id().as_local()`.
Do not follow constructors as recursion edges; they always have MIR but "Constructor functions cannot cause a query cycle."
Do not follow `InstanceKind::Intrinsic(_) | InstanceKind::Virtual(..)` or `FnPtrAddrShim`, and skip items where `!tcx.is_mir_available(callee.def_id())`.
Do not build MIR for incompletely instantiated drop glue; the code skips `DropGlue`, `FutureDropPollShim`, `AsyncDropGlue`, and `AsyncDropGlueCtorShim` when `callee.has_param()`.

When the recursion limit is exceeded the code returns `true` for that branch ("Pessimistically assume that there could be recursion"), so callers must treat that as a cycle rather than as absence of recursion.

The cached query result is an arena-cached `UnordSet<LocalDefId>` with `cache_on_disk_if { true }`; changing the set's contents without respecting caching could make inlining decisions differ across compilation modes.
analysis.testStrategy: Construct Rust test crates that force MIR inlining to consider cyclic local callees, especially mutual recursion and generic functions whose call edges resolve differently at different instantiations. Compile with MIR inlining enabled (and, separately, force-inlining of a candidate) and verify there is no query-cycle ICE while the expected function is or is not inlined. Include cases for constructors, intrinsics/virtual calls, function-pointer shims, MIR-less/extern functions, and parameterized drop glue so `should_recurse`'s exclusions are exercised. Because no compiler was built for this task, do not claim that any test was executed or that the behavior was reproduced; these are source-derived testing strategies only.
